description: I’m building a visor-HUD tool that plans a safe, mobility-aware EVA route across Mars boxwork terrain, with real NASA terrain data, science stops and a radiation and time budget. My youtube channel is: @wynspace.
summary:
VISOR is a browser-based planner for the first astronauts to walk on Mars. It plans a two-person EVA across the boxwork ridges of Gale crater, through the two sites NASA's Curiosity rover drilled there.

The problem: orbital maps are the only maps of most of Mars, and at walking scale they can be wrong. VISOR checks the map against what Curiosity measured on the same ground. At 85 rover stops, the 1 m HiRISE elevation model reads slopes about 3.4° steeper than the rover's own tilt sensors. VISOR applies that measured correction to the route and marks where the map can and cannot be trusted.

What planners get:
- A route within the slope limit, with walk-back time to safety from any point
- Station science, sample bags and chemistry from NASA sources
- Weather and radiation Curiosity recorded, plus daylight and twilight timing
- Radio line of sight with a relay position
- A first-person 3D rehearsal of the whole EVA
details:
What it does

VISOR is a mission planner for one of the first walks humans might take on Mars. I set it in Gale crater, on the boxwork ridges of Mount Sharp, because Curiosity has just driven there and drilled two rock samples ten metres apart: Valle de la Luna in a hollow and Nevado Sajama on a ridge. VISOR plans a two-person EVA (a "Marswalk") through those sites and the stops around them.

The idea behind it is simple: an orbital map is a guess until something has stood on the ground. The 1 m HiRISE elevation model is the best map of this area, but nobody had checked it at the scale of a person walking. Curiosity carries tilt sensors, so wherever it parked, we know the real slope under its wheels. I compared the map with the rover at 85 stops. The map reads slopes about 3.4° steeper than the ground Curiosity measured (median difference 4.4°). The correction also held up when tested on rover stops it was not fitted to. VISOR applies that measured correction to the route, and it shows the planner where the map is reliable and where it is not.

How it works for a planner

You open it in a browser. No install, no login. You see the 25 cm HiRISE photo with the planned route, coloured by steepness. You can:

- Add, remove or drag stations; the route re-plans in a moment under your slope limit and walking speed.

- See the walk-back time to the exit from any point, and which stretches are out of radio sight of the exit (80% of the published route). VISOR can place a relay person on high ground that brings the route in contact from 20% to 88%.

- Open each station to see its science question, sample bags, Curiosity's own photo and 360° view from that spot, and the chemistry ChemCam and APXS measured nearby, all linked to NASA sources.

- Check conditions: the weather REMS recorded, the radiation RAD measured, and where the sun will be, with daylight, twilight (up to 2 hours, per NASA) and night across the whole 6-hour EVA.

- Switch to Walk mode and rehearse the EVA in first-person 3D with two astronauts, a mission clock, the real sun, and Curiosity standing where it parked.

- Print a cue card for each station, keep a log during the EVA, and share or export the plan (link, JSON, CSV, GeoJSON).

Benefits and intended impact

Most planning tools show a route. VISOR also shows how far to trust it. A planner can see that the map says 22.8° at Valle de la Luna while Curiosity measured 6.8°, or that at Río Frío the ground is steeper than the map shows, and plan around both. The method is not tied to this site: anywhere a rover has driven, its tilt data can check the map the same way. That matters for choosing safe first walks on Mars, and for making NASA's rover data useful to people who are not rover scientists.

How it is creative

It treats the rover as a surveyor for the astronauts who come after it. VISOR builds on earlier comparisons of elevation models with rover tilt; what it adds is turning that comparison into the plan itself: the correction goes into the route, the HUD and the trust layers, alongside walk-back time, relay placement, daylight and a full rehearsal you can share as a link.

Factors I considered

- Honesty about limits. I wrote every test rule before running it and kept the result either way. Some failed, and VISOR says so: the 1 m map cannot resolve the 1–2 m ridges, and my attempt to trace ridges from the photo did not pass its check. Assumptions (20° slope limit, 0.6 m/s walking speed, 1.7 m eye height) are labelled wherever they appear.

- Cross-checks. The sun model agrees with NASA Mars Trek's sun service to within 0.3°, and sunrise and sunset agree with the REMS feed to within 2 minutes over 323 sols.

- Safety first. Walk-back time, rescue time, radio contact and twilight warnings sit next to the science.

- Usability. Numbers come first and long text is folded away. Meaning is never shown by colour alone.

- Performance. Planning runs in a background Web Worker, and loading retries stalled downloads on its own.

Tools

Rust and the Bevy 0.20 game engine, compiled to WebAssembly and rendered with WebGL2; Leptos for the interface; Trunk for the web build; a Python pipeline (NumPy, SciPy, rasterio) to process the NASA data into a small validated bundle; headless Chrome tests; GitHub Actions and GitHub Pages for hosting. Built on a Windows laptop with an RTX 3050. I used an SI (AI) assistant, Claude by Anthropic, for research, coding and writing help, and Qwen3-TTS for the demo video's narration; both are disclosed in the repo and the video.
